title: Comments of Eolian, L.P. in support of Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s High Impact Large Load and High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment Processes under ER26-247.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
BEFORE THE
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

							)
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.			)		Docket No. ER26-247-000
)

COMMENTS OF EOLIAN L.P. IN SUPPORT OF SPP’S HILL AND HILLGA PROCESSES

	Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure, Eolian L.P. (Eolian) respectfully submits comments in support of Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (SPP) proposal to adopt a High Impact Large Load (HILL) process and High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (HILLGA) process (the “SPP filing”). As discussed herein, Eolian is a developer of energy generation and load projects, including battery energy storage systems (BESS), that anticipates developing resources to serve HILLs via SPP’s HILLGA process. Eolian recognizes that SPP must continue its reforms in order to integrate large loads reliably and affordably into SPP’s footprint, including in particular adopting workable modifications to its existing transmission services requirements for HILLs served by one or more HILLGA generating facilities. Eolian supports this filing as an important step forward and a just and reasonable approach to studying large loads and the generating facilities that seek to serve them. 
Eolian submits these comments to address the HILLGA process. Specifically, as a prospective interconnection customer that plans to participate in the HILLGA process, Eolian contends that the interconnection process is just and reasonable, not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and does not violate open access principles. Eolian provides legal analysis that affords a second, supplemental basis for the Commission’s approval of the HILLGA process as consistent with its open access precedent.  
Finally, to avoid any risk of the proposal appearing to result in undue discrimination, Eolian requests that, in approving the HILLGA proposal, the Commission require SPP to clarify that the new pathway for HILLGA resources to serve particular HILLs does not remove or limit existing pathways for non HILLGA resources to serve particular HILLs. More particularly, FERC should require SPP to clarify that its tariff revisions do not restrict non HILLGA resources from specifically serving HILL load for purposes of demonstrating adequate designated or planned resources pursuant to the relevant transmission service study processes set forth in Attachments AQ and AX. 
EOLIAN’S INTEREST
Eolian Plans to Participate in the HILLGA Process to Serve HILLs.
Eolian develops renewable energy technologies and energy storage assets throughout the United States and has originated 27 GW of operating generating and storage capacity to date, including 2.1 GW of proposed battery storage with executed Generator Interconnection Agreements (GIAs) in SPP and an additional 1.1 GW of proposed surplus generation capacity in SPP with completed studies awaiting surplus GIAs. Eolian and our partners have developed projects supporting large loads in multiple regions across the United States. Should SPP’s filing be approved, Eolian expects to participate in the HILLGA process to develop storage resources to serve large loads.  
THE HILLGA PROCESS IS NOT UNDULY DISCRIMINATORY OR PREFERENTIAL AND COMPLIES WITH OPEN ACCESS.
SPP seeks the Commission’s approval of the HILLGA process as an independent entity variation to the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Procedures, and argues that the HILLGA process meets the legal standard for approval of an independent entity variation because it (a) does not disadvantage existing SPP interconnection customers; (b) is narrowly tailored to address a pressing problem; and (c) encourages faster, more efficient interconnection consistent with one of the key goals of Order No. 2023. Eolian supports SPP’s assertion that the HILLGA process is just and reasonable, not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and complies with the Commission’s open access principles, and provides additional grounds for the Commission to reach such a finding. 
Interconnection customers have comparable access to the HILLGA process. 
The Commission must carefully scrutinize proposals that “create barriers to entry for specific classes of interconnection customers or that create unduly discriminatory priority access to the generator interconnection process” to ensure that such proposal meet the statutory standard and do not violate open access principles. Here, the HILLGA process affords a faster generator interconnection process compared to SPP’s standard generator interconnection process, the Definitive Interconnection System Impact Study (DISIS). Importantly, however, SPP’s proposal affords comparable access to the expedited interconnection process to any interconnection customer that proposes to develop a generating facility in order to support a HILL. That is, SPP has proposed objective eligibility requirements to participate in HILLGA, as set forth in Attachment BB Section 3.1.3 (HILLGA Requirements), that are limited to ensuring the proposed generating facility is technically capable of serving a particular HILL. Specifically, SPP’s proposal would require the HILLGA request to match the MW load amount associated with the HILL (Section 3.1.2(2)), be located in the same local area as the HILL (Section 3.1.2(5)), and be capable of matching the ramp rate of the HILL and maintaining the ramp rate for a sufficient duration to be able to serve the HILL (Section 3.1.2(5)(a)(ii)). Interconnection customers thus have a comparable ability to compete for the opportunity to serve HILLs (i.e., to the same extent that such opportunities to compete are available in a particular Load Responsible Entity (LRE) jurisdiction), and any proposed generating facility technically capable of doing so may then access HILLGA. As a result, the HILLGA process does not conflict with the Commission’s open access requirements.        
The HILLGA process is subject to inherent, practical limitations. 
The Commission has recognized that access to a different interconnection process may not conflict with open access principles where that specialized process entails inherent practical limitations on its use, and that process results in substantial potential benefits. For that reason, SPP’s proposal would not raise open access concerns even assuming arguendo that it did not provide comparable ability for interconnection customers to compete to participate in the HILLGA process. Much like the surplus generator interconnection process, the more limited purpose of and more limited interconnection service provided by the process results in inherent, practical limits on the use of the HILLGA process.
SPP explains that the optional HILLGA process differs from the standardized generator interconnection process in that it aims to enable interconnection of the resource solely for the purpose of serving a HILL at the outset, rather than to enable interconnection for the purpose of serving SPP load more broadly. Correspondingly, the HILLGA process results in “interconnection rights solely for that Generating Facility to serve the HILL, not the SPP Balancing Authority as a whole.” The interconnection rights acquired through HILLGA are further limited to a five-year period from the resource’s commercial operation date, after which a resource must complete the standardized generator interconnection process in order to continue operation. These requirements impose several inherent limits on the use of the HILLGA process. First, access to the HILLGA process is limited by the number of HILLs developed in SPP that lack sufficient designated or planned resources to serve their needs. Second, the total capacity that is developed through the HILLGA process is limited to a level needed to serve such HILLs. Third, HILLGA resources must be located in near electrical (and therefore likely geographical) proximity to a HILL, which inherently limits the number of generating facilities that may qualify. And fourth, it is likely that only a subset of developers would find time- and customer-limited interconnection rights workable for their business models. Together, these constraints constitute practical limitations on the use of HILLGA.
At the same time, SPP describes the significant value of this limited purpose interconnection process. Absent an opportunity for expedited development of resources to serve HILLs, the economic and national security benefits of integration of these large loads will be delayed in SPP. Under SPP’s existing tariff, a HILL (like other loads) cannot receive a delivery point and be subject to study until it has sufficient designated or planned resources. But as SPP explains, large load customers are requesting faster deployment timelines for generation supporting large loads than typical interconnection study timelines. The HILLGA process helps to address that gap, facilitating the timely integration of large loads. By enabling a HILLGA generator access to limited interconnection rights to solely serve a HILL (and studying the generator in light of that more limited service), the generating facility will be able to enter into commercial operation more rapidly, both due to the shorter study time and the avoided construction of network upgrades that could be necessary if the generator served SPP load more broadly. And, as a result, the HILL will be able to be studied and enter into operation more rapidly.  
The HILLGA process is distinguishable from ERAS.
The Commission approved SPP ERAS as a “one-time” process to address near-term resource adequacy concerns. Because the HILLGA process is justified by distinct Commission precedent, as described above, that pre-dates the Commission’s approval of SPP ERAS and similar one-off expedited generator interconnection processes in other RTO/ISOs to address resource adequacy concerns, the Commission need not assess the HILLGA process against the legal standard that the Commission applied to such proposals to ensure that they were sufficiently tailored to meet resource adequacy challenges. Eolian nevertheless notes that a number of features distinguish the HILLGA process from the aspects of SPP ERAS that raised concerns among commentors:
The HILLGA process results in different and more limited interconnection service from the standardized queue process; whereas ERAS and DISIS interconnection customers received the same type of interconnection service.

The customer-limited and time-limited nature of Load Limited Resource Interconnection Service (LLRIS) (and corresponding focus of the HILLGA study on localized transmission system impacts caused by injection to serve only the HILL) constrain the degree to which HILLGA requests interact with interconnection requests in DISIS. In contrast, the ERAS process studied impacts assuming deliverability to SPP load as a whole.  

The HILLGA process does not condition eligibility on state support or LRE selection.    


SPP SHOULD CONTINUE REFORMS TO TRANSMISSION SERVICE REQUIREMENTS TO ENSURE JUST AND REASONABLE RATES AS UNPRECEDENTED LARGE LOAD GROWTH PERSISTS
SPP acknowledges that it continues its work with stakeholders to develop other mechanisms to support the timely and reliable interconnection and operation of HILLs. SPP’s current proposal, while not a complete solution to the challenges posed by the potentially exponential growth of load over the next five years, is an important improvement to existing load and generator interconnection processes. The Commission should both approve SPP’s filing as a just and reasonable approach and urge SPP to continue its ongoing reform efforts.  
SPP’s existing transmission service requirements remain a key barrier to ensuring just and reasonable rates in the face of unprecedented load growth. As SPP acknowledges, “neither the HILL study process outlined in Attachment BA nor the HILLGA process set forth in Attachment BB will result in a grant of transmission service for the HILL. A customer must still request transmission service using one of SPP’s existing mechanisms to receive transmission service.” Likewise, “the HILLGA process does not provide any type of transmission service for the Generating Facility to serve the HILL.” 
But SPP’s existing transmission service provisions would not allow a transmission customer to serve HILLs that lack designated Network Resources with Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS). NITS is defined as service utilizing Network Resources to serve Network Load. A Network Resource, in turn, does not include resources that “cannot be called upon to meet the Network Customer’s Network Load on a non-interruptible basis,” and therefore would not appear to encompass a HILLGA resource, which only obtains limited interconnection service to serve the HILL rather than broader Network Load. SPP additionally takes the position that, in order to process applications for NITS, which requires a listing of Network Loads and the Network Resources implicated in their service, the transmission customer must match Network Loads with a commensurate supply of Network Resources. SPP thus takes the position that “the Network Customer must have enough Network Resources to serve their Network Load.” Absent further reforms, a transmission customer would appear unable to add the load for a HILL that is served by HILLGA generating facilities as Network Load served under its NITS agreements, even though the HILL has been appropriately studied pursuant to Attachment AX, the HILLGA resource has been appropriately studied pursuant to the HILLGA process, and the transmission customer, in fact, has adequate resources with deliverability to the HILL.
As a result, absent further reforms, the HILLGA resource would need to be further studied for deliverability to all of SPP load in order to qualify as a Network Resource, or additional Network Resources would need to be designated, in order for a HILL served by a HILLGA to qualify for NITS. But in a time of exponential load growth, studying resources to be deliverable in a manner that they will not, in fact, operate (nor need to operate in order to reliably serve particular loads) greatly and unnecessarily increases the time to develop needed supply, slowing down integration of large loads and driving up the costs of new capacity as supply lags demand. Such study assumptions likewise increase the likelihood that significant network upgrades are called for prior to the interconnection of loads and the resources developed to serve them, further delaying the integration of large loads. Again, such network upgrades may be unnecessary if local resources are configured to solely serve a large load. SPP’s existing transmission service provisions appear to limit SPP’s ability to make LLRIS a sensible option to facilitate more rapid, reliable integration of large loads, available on more than a short-term basis.
Consistent with the Department of Energy’s recent Large Load Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, SPP should advance reforms that would tailor transmission service requirements to better reflect the operations of large loads and the resources developed to serve them.
SPP SHOULD clarify that non hillga resources may serve as Designated or planned generation to serve a hill for purposes of attachmentS aQ and ax
SPP’s proposal provides a more particular arrangement by which a transmission customer may identify generation (the HILLGA resource) that will serve the needs of its additional load (the HILL) for purposes of study under Attachments AQ, AX, or Z1 and ultimately to obtain transmission service under its tariff. While Eolian does not understand SPP to intend to limit resources that are not studied via HILLGA from being able to commercially contract with a HILL to serve that same function, SPP can clarify that its tariff revisions do not restrict non HILLGA resources from specifically serving HILL load for purposes of demonstrating adequate designated or planned resources pursuant to the relevant transmission service study. Such clarification would remove any doubt that the proposal would result in undue discrimination among HILLGA and non HILLGA resources that are equally technically capable of serving a HILL’s needs and thereby supporting a transmission customer’s ability to establish transmission service for that load. 
Because it creates a new interconnection process for “generating Resources that are specifically identified for and limited to serving a HILL,” SPP’s newly proposed HILLGA process creates the potential for misinterpretation of existing tariff provisions as applied to the newly defined HILL load category. As SPP explains, “SPP’s HILL process set forth in Attachment BA, in concert with the existing study processes in Attachment AQ and AX, will provide a delivery point for the HILL.” As specified in SPP’s tariff proposal, the HILLGA process provides for the HILLGA Customer (i.e., the generation developer) to indicate the particular HILL that it will serve. The proposal contemplates that, via SPP’s existing tariff processes, the HILLGA generating facility will then support the interconnection of the HILL and be designated by the applicable Transmission Customer to serve the new load through the applicable transmission service request process. 
SPP should clarify that, in providing for a new generator interconnection process that requires HILLGA Customers to indicate that they will serve a particular HILL, SPP does not in any way restrict the ability of Interconnection Customers that have obtained or are requesting Network Resource Interconnection Service (NRIS) through the DISIS process to enter into similar commercial arrangements to serve particular HILLs. SPP should make clear that where such arrangements exist, they may form the basis for the applicable resource to be listed either as a “planned resource” in an Attachment AX request, or a Designated Resource in an Attachment AQ request. This clarification is required in order to ensure that the SPP tariff does not provide HILLGA resources with any undue advantage over NRIS resources with respect to providing service to HILLs.

					Respectfully submitted,
